In Mind Up!, you start with a line of cards on the table, with as many cards as players. Each turn, players pick a card from their hand and simultaneously reveal it to make a new line, ordered from the lowest to the highest card. Each player then takes the card in the previous line at the same position as the one they just played, adding it to their tableau. These cards will score points at the end of the round, depending on their color and the order they were picked. After being scored, they become the player's hand for the next round. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary A game of Mind Up! plays in 3 rounds, each being played over several turns. Each turn, you compete with the other players to obtain the cards in the center of the table. Guess what your opponents will play, choose the right number from your hand so that you can place your card next to the card you want to take! The card deck is made of 60 cards, from 1 to 60, with 12 cards in each of the 5 colors. Contents 1 Gameplay 2 End of round and Scoring 3 Variant: Bonus Objectives 3.1 Effects of Objective cards Gameplay The game is divided in 3 rounds. At the beginning of a round, each player receives 7 cards (or 8/9 in the 2nd/3rd round). The order of set of scoring cards (1 to 5 yellow cards) is randomly selected and is the same for each player. Finally, as many cards as players are revealed, serving as the first prizes. Each turn, there are X revealed prize cards on the table, for X players. Players simultaneously select a card from their hand and reveal them. Whoever played the lowest card gains the lowest prize card, then whoever played the 2nd lowest gains the 2nd lowest prize card, and so on in ascending order. The prize card you gain is placed in your scoring row. - If there already are cards of the same color in your scoring row, the new card is added to the column containing that color. - If there aren't any card of the same color in your scoring row, the new card is added to the leftmost empty column. Note : The first card you get will always be placed in the leftmost column. The cards which have been played during this turn become the prize cards for the following turn. The round ends when players only have 1 card left in their hand. That card is added to their scoring row, following placement rules. End of round and Scoring At the end of a round, each card in your scoring row grants you as many points as the number on the scoring card at the top of its column. Then, the bonus (yellow bubbles on your scored cards) and malus (red bubbles) are added or substracted to your score. At the end of the 1st and 2nd round, the scoring rows are reset for the next round. Players receive new cards (8 or 9 depending on the round). The starting prize cards are the played cards during the last turn of the previous round. The player with the highest total is the winner. In case of a tie, the winner is the player who scored the most points in the last round. Variant: Bonus Objectives At the start of each round, a Bonus Objective card is randomly revealed. When scoring points, if the scored cards meet the indicated condition, the bonus or malus of this objective card is added (or substracted) from your score. A new Objective card is then revealed for the following round. Depending on setup choices, there can be multiple objective cards per round, up to 5 per round. If you play with 3+ objective cards, they are not changed between rounds. Effects of Objective cards A : +2 if you have 1 or 3 orange cards A : -2 if your orange cards are the scoring column of value 1 or 2 B : +2 if you have 2 or 4 blue cards B : +2 if blue is the color you have the most cards of (or if blue is tied) C : -2 if you are the player with the least pink cards (or are tied for the least pink cards) C : +2 if you are the player with the most pink cards (or are tied for the most pink cards) D : +2 if there are no card on the right of your green cards D : +2 if your green cards are the scoring column of value 4 or 5 E

[Rating: 2/10] 6 nimmt! but with a more convoluted scoring system, which does it no favours really as you can't really concentrate on what other players might be collecting or try to anticipate their plays at all, making it a strictly less interesting version of a game I'm already not grabbed by.

[Rating: 2/10] Also known as Shit Nimmt! Just play that instead. Too random, no way to read the board state or predict play as the distribution of the cards is too broad, and is so balanced that no matter what you do you more or less end up in the same region of points.

[Rating: 3/10] BGA. It's sort of a blind auction to get scoring cards. There's strategy, but the game decisions feel kind of meaningless.

[Rating: 3/10] If you wanted to like this but didn't, try 6 nimmt!/Take 5 or Turn the Tide. They are a similar genre but better.

[Rating: 3.5/10] I'm not against mixing a variant of Mandala's scoring with the gameplay from the second half of For Sale, but Mind Up lacks something to anchor mindful play, especially in the early game when nobody has settled onto a couple suits yet. ("But look, this card has a flat +1 point on it!" is not enough.) [Rating: 4/10] Mind sans Mgmt  D’une sobriété toute allemande, ce jeu pourrait sortir de chez Amigo, mais non, Il est françaiiiiiis monsieur ! Jeu de collection de couleurs, il faut prendre des cartes sur un marché en posant des valeurs : la plus petite prend la première carte etc. A vous de mettre la valeur qui vous permette de prendre la couleur qui vous intéresse. Ces nouvelles cartes deviennent alors le marché du tour prochain. Une fois la manche terminée, on compte les points et on rejoue avec les mêmes cartes. On voit bien l’idée mais on a peu de contrôle sur le déroulé. Au final on est avec un produit

[Rating: 4/10] This is a card drafting game where players bid for cards in a simultaneous reveal. The goal is to score extra points by collecting sets of suits, and your collections in one round form the hand of bid-cards for the next round.  It's a combination of mechanisms I've seen in plenty of other games, but the work of Stefan Dorra stands out: [i]For Sale[/i] and [i]Turn the Tide[/i] have the simultaneous reveal element, but without suits or set collection (or those annoying +1, -1 elements on many cards). [Rating: 4/10] i like simple little cardgames.  but this is so MEH.  there is a lot of fun cardplay - "trickish": play a card face down, put them all in order, take the one in the same spot your played card ends up in.  THE APPEARANCE OF CONTROL is strong. sure, you can card and colour count, but what's the point.  there is so little control, even if you want to devote that much effort to such a light game.  and why bother.  play The Crew, No Thanks, No Merci... or many many others.  MEH.

[Rating: 4/10] Présenté comme une alternative au "6 qui prend", alias Take Five. On est plutôt amusés par les petits filler games, en apéro ou dessert d'un gros jeu. Mais là, c'est tellement aléatoire qu'on attendra l'EHPAD pour y rejouer.

[Rating: 4/10] Played at Spiel 23, seemed to be very basic decisions, even for a filler, it was too automatic. The scoring reminded me of Mandala, but obviously with more players. With Mandala, there’s a since of tension around who & when the mandala scores, which adds to the card scoring system nicely. Here, it seems instead to have a kind of memory element, trying to track what cards your opponents have taken in previous rounds, which I didn’t really enjoy.
